web.title: Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular Apps
web.description: A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it.   Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly.   Security firm pwn.ai  showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396 , was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks.   Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. web.title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats
web.description: A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse  user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown.   The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts.   The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec , the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes.   Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer.   There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach.

web.title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys
web.description: A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME , the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG.   The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions.   The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975 , affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program.   Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages.
